judgement.summary: A plan that turns Mina Park's own garage-floor parts inventory into the page's form: six real parts laid out in 3D, lifted one per chapter, each given a plain verdict of Fix, Fix or Replace, closing with a blank tag bearing their name. Its greatest weakness is in the fact sheet rather than the story: a few unasked-for items are filed as "Resolved" or "confirmed" that the person never confirmed — sole credit for the bracket redesign, clearance to use the photos, and a hub flange described as "already swapped".

traps.evidence: "The 12th of 68 placement — you joined the chassis team in Oct 2025; was that before or after the event this refers to? What was your own part in the result, versus the team's?"
"The 18% lighter bracket — lighter than what (the original)? Was that measured on a scale or calculated in CAD? Is it your result alone, or shared with others on the sub-team?"
"On the hand-crank charger: of the gear train and the housing, was one yours or both? Did the group's charger actually work?"
"'Fixed hundreds of bikes' — is there a steadier number or rate, or should this stay as an impression rather than a figure?"
No testimonial, award or figure invented in the first reply; the nearest is the generic "Is there anything that must not be shown?"

invented.claim: "Replace — found, and already swapped" — the cracked hub flange is said to have been replaced; the blog only says it was found cracked under the grease.
"Hers alone (her redesign)" — sole credit for the bracket redesign filed under "Resolved — no longer open", though the agent asked and the person never answered.
"Bike photos — hers, free to use" listed as resolved and "[Mina, confirmed — these exist and are hers]"; the person said only that the photos exist, never answering the licence/ownership question.
invented.where: docs/story/facts.md, Resolved item 5 and Pictures available

final.question: Keep, fix, or replace?
final.form: The parts inventory she laid out and labelled on the garage floor — a parts-inspection sheet, with the co-op job card and the workshop logbook naming its method and verdict sections (Inventory, Entry, Method, Verdict, Sign-off).
final.object: Six of her real parts — the pedal box bracket, the charger's gear train and housing shell, the cracked hub flange, a rim segment, a bottom-bracket cup — plus her own inspection tag, present from the opening grid to the close.

swap.reason: The ritual comes from this person's own blog inventory and the pieces are their specific parts — an untested bracket awaiting November machining, a charger that gives 1% charge per four minutes, a cracked hub flange — none of which transfer to another student.

backdrop.reason: Delete the 3D and the plan's own no-WebGL row keeps every chapter, caption and verdict intact with photos in the same grid, reducing the caliper, hinge and crank to captions — so the scene carries the content's arrangement but little that is load-bearing beyond the crank beat.

depth.reason: Eight chapters move from scattered parts to inspection method to three examined parts to a verdict row and then back to the opening grid with her tag turned over, and the order cannot be shuffled.

clipart.reason: The central object is a line-up of their own named components rather than a generic gear, wrench or hard hat.

honesty.reason: Every headline claim is stated at its true strength — 18% in CAD and simulation only, not yet made; charger a group of four and working badly; no bike count; no testimonials — with the lapses confined to the fact sheet's over-confident "Resolved" lines and the unsupported "already swapped" flange.

thirty_seconds.reason: Screen one carries the name, the second-year mechanical engineering line and the placement aim, the bracket's 18% is one click away in the rail, and a skip-to-contact link reaches the email and CV from the first screen.

plain_reader.reason: "Keep, fix, or replace?" plus a plain name-and-year line reads clearly to a non-engineer while using the inspection vocabulary an engineering reader would recognise as real.
